newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen higher at opening.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen higher at opening.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to move higher at the open Tuesday after registering their first rise in nearly a week yesterday.

The market will remain volatile, however, and the opening will give little clue as to the close. Analysts said they expected continued turbulence in a week larded with important economic data and the second round of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
They said that yesterday's upward move was due to buying in index funds which pushed blue chips higher.

"At this point in time, it looks as though we will have a firm opening," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "Yesterday, we saw the same old movement of index funds into the old Nifty-Fifty stocks.
"The breadth was even keel, and it was a Dow rally of the same old stocks. They langusih for a few days, and then the index funds move them."

Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said that he expected to see strength in the high techs today but that the real focus of attention was this Friday's employment report for February.
"In the long term, the market will move much higher. In the short term, there are still questions, and one of them will be answered on Friday," Cardillo said.
"If we get an acceleration in hourly wages, my guess is that the Fed will pull the trigger and raise rates. Greenspan might give us a pre-emptive strike."
He said that the stock market was in the process of discounting an interest rate hike.
January leading indicators and new home sales are due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 135.65 points, or 0.74 percent, at 18,564.78.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 46.8 at 4353.9.

Among U.S. stocks traded in London, oil drilling shares were among the best performers in London. Baker Hughes Inc gained $1/4 to $35, Schlumberger Ltd rose $1/4 to $98-3/4 and Halliburton Co climbed $1/4 to $62.
The dollar hit an nearly three-year against the mark in Tokyo and was firm in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly stronger, with the long bond up 8/32 to yield 6.81 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Wall Street is playing "pick the survivors" with paging companies. It said the companies' promises of two-way beepers and Internet-linked pages once made them among the hottest communications groups around. Some investors are now just fed up with the group for promising too much.
The New York Times Market Place writes that with the Dow industrials and stock prices hovering near record highs, experts say this could be one of the biggest years ever for stock splits.

So far this year Boeing Co , DuPont Co, Exxon Corp, International Business Machines Corp and Philip Morris Cos Inc have all announced splits, and Intel Corp, BankAmerica Corp and Bristol-Myers Squibb are among those scheduling splits.
